questiontext.text:
Goal

Write a Python file that binds three names and prints a four line station report.

How this works in Python

In Java the smallest program that prints a line still needs a class and a main method.

public class Logger {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String site = "Kaikoura";
        System.out.println("Site: " + site);
    }
}

Python needs none of that. The file itself is the program. Every line you write at the left margin runs from top to bottom the moment you run the file.

site = "Kaikoura"
print("Site:", site)

Four things changed. Read them one at a time.

  • Java declares a variable by putting a type in front of the name. Python writes the name, an =, and the value. There is no type, no var, and no keyword. channels = 3 is the whole declaration. Python calls this binding a name.
  • No line ends with a semicolon. You write one statement per line, and the newline ends it.
  • print is Python's System.out.println. It takes several values separated by commas, puts one space between them, and adds a newline at the end. You never join the values with +.
  • # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line, the way // does in Java.

Python names its types differently. Text in quotes is a str, short for string. A whole number is an int. A number with a decimal point is a float. You never write any of those three words in your code. Python reads the value and works out the type for you.

Python names variables differently too. Words go in lower case and join with underscores, so Java's sampleRate becomes sample_rate.

Your task
  • Bind site to the string Kaikoura.
  • Bind channels to the int 3.
  • Bind sample_rate to the float 2.5.
  • Print the four lines below with one call to print for each. The third line is blank, and a bare print() with no arguments prints a blank line.
SEISMIC LOGGER
==============

Site: Kaikoura Channels: 3 Rate: 2.5

You pass when your output matches character for character, blank line included. The tests print extra lines underneath your output, so expect your banner at the top of every result.

Rules
  • Do not write a semicolon anywhere in the file. The checker rejects it on sight.
  • Do not write a type before a name. channels = 3 is the whole declaration.
  • Do not write a type after a name either. channels: int = 3 fails the same checker.
  • Pass the three names to print. Do not retype their values as literals inside the call.
  • Build the summary with one call to print and commas between the arguments.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

question.answerpreload: # The file is the program. Write at the left margin, with no class and no main. # TODO: bind site, channels and sample_rate, then print the banner and the summary line.
question.answer:
# Station details site = "Kaikoura" channels = 3 sample_rate = 2.5
print("SEISMIC LOGGER") print("==============") print() print("Site:", site, "Channels:", channels, "Rate:", sample_rate)

expected.text:
SEISMIC LOGGER ==============
Site: Kaikoura Channels: 3 Rate: 2.5 --- end of report ---

testcode.text: import inspect, sys src = inspect.getsource(sys.modules['__main__']) assert chr(59) not in src, "rule broken: no semicolons" colon = chr(58) for word in ("int", "str", "float", "bool"): assert colon + " " + word not in src, "rule broken: no type before or after a name" print(site, channels, sample_rate)

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write the body of a classify function that prints one word for a pressure reading.

How this works in Python

The first tier of this topic gave you print and name binding. Those same statements now move inside a block.

Java marks a block with braces. The indentation is there for the reader, and the compiler ignores it.

if (pressure <= 0 || pressure > 2000) {
    System.out.println("FAULT");
} else if (pressure < 900) {
    System.out.println("LOW");
} else {
    System.out.println("HIGH");
}

Python has no braces. The indentation is the block, and the parser enforces it.

if pressure <= 0 or pressure > 2000:
    print("FAULT")
elif pressure < 900:
    print("LOW")
else:
    print("HIGH")

Five differences matter here.

  • The header line ends with a colon. Leave the colon off and Python reports a SyntaxError.
  • The condition takes no parentheses.
  • Java's else if becomes one word, elif.
  • The boolean operators are words. Write and, or and not. The symbols &&, || and ! are not part of Python.
  • Indent every line of one block by the same amount. Four spaces is the convention. A line indented by the wrong amount raises an IndentationError before any of your code runs.

In Python def starts a function, so the line def classify(pressure): declares a function called classify that takes one argument named pressure.

Once the tests pass, take one line of your block and add a single extra space in front of it. Run it again and read the IndentationError. Then put the line back. Java ignores that space. Python treats it as the structure of your program.

Your task
  • Write the body of classify(pressure) indented four spaces under the header already in the answer box. Print exactly one word for each pressure value, testing the branches in the order below.
  • Print FAULT when the pressure is 0 or below, or above 2000. Write that branch as one condition joined with or.
  • Print LOW when the pressure is below 900.
  • Print NORMAL when the pressure is 900 to 1100 inclusive.
  • Print HIGH for anything else.

You pass when each call prints one of those four words and nothing else.

Rules
  • Do not type { or } anywhere in your answer.
  • Do not put parentheses round a condition.
  • Spell the operators out as words. The checker fails on && and ||.
  • Write elif. A nested if inside the else passes the tests and fails this exercise.
  • Indent with four spaces and never press Tab. Mixing the two raises TabError, not a style warning.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

question.answerpreload: def classify(pressure): # TODO: print FAULT, LOW, NORMAL or HIGH with an if, elif, elif, else chain

testcode.text: classify(899) classify(900) classify(1100) classify(1101) classify(0) classify(2000)

expected.text: LOW NORMAL NORMAL HIGH FAULT HIGH

testcode.text: import inspect src = inspect.getsource(classify) amp = chr(38) assert "elif" in src, "rule broken: use elif, not a nested if" assert amp + amp not in src, "rule broken: spell out and" assert "||" not in src, "rule broken: spell out or" assert "{" not in src and "}" not in src, "rule broken: no braces" assert "\t" not in src, "rule broken: four spaces, never a tab" assert "if (" not in src, "rule broken: no parentheses round the condition" classify(42)

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write the body of a station_report function that grades a pressure, works out a status, and prints a report block.

How this works in Python

A Java method that builds a report declares its variables first, assigns to them inside a branch, and glues the output together with +.

static void stationReport(String site, int pressure, int channels, int days) {
    String grade;
    if (pressure <= 0 || pressure > 2000) {
        grade = "FAULT";
    } else if (pressure < 900) {
        grade = "LOW";
    } else {
        grade = "OK";
    }
    System.out.println("Pressure: " + pressure + " " + grade);
}

Python drops the declaration line. A name comes into being the moment you assign to it, and a name assigned inside a branch is still there after the branch ends.

if pressure <= 0 or pressure > 2000:
    grade = "FAULT"
else:
    grade = "OK"

print("Pressure:", pressure, grade)

Three things to carry into this exercise.

  • Assigning inside a branch is the whole declaration. Python has nothing to match Java's bare String grade; line, and you do not want one.
  • == between two strings compares the characters. Java's == compares references, which is why Java makes you write grade.equals("FAULT"). In Python grade == "FAULT" is the right form and the only one.
  • A bare print() prints a blank line. print("Status:", status) puts one space between the two values, so you never join them with +.

Order decides the answer twice over. A station on 2001 with six healthy channels comes out OFFLINE, because the grade is settled before the channel count is looked at. A station on 899 with three channels calibrated 30 days ago comes out LOW and ONLINE. Neither boundary trips, because 30 is not more than 30 and 3 is not fewer than 3.

The earlier tiers of this topic supply everything you need. Name binding and print came from the first tier, and the colon header with its indented block came from the second.

Your task
  • Write the body of station_report(site, pressure, channels, days_since_calibration) indented four spaces under the header already in the answer box.
  • Work out the grade from the pressure and bind it to a name, testing these branches in order.
    • FAULT when the pressure is 0 or below, or above 2000.
    • LOW when the pressure is below 900.
    • NORMAL when the pressure is 900 to 1100 inclusive.
    • HIGH for anything else.
  • Work out the status from the grade you bound and the other two values, testing these branches in order too.
    • OFFLINE when the grade is FAULT, or the station has 0 channels or fewer.
    • DEGRADED when the last calibration was more than 30 days ago, or the station has fewer than 3 channels.
    • ONLINE for anything else.
  • Print the report shown below. The first block is a call, the second is the exact output of that call, and the sixth line of it is blank.
  • Print the third block underneath the status line when the status is anything other than ONLINE.
station_report("Kaikoura", 1000, 4, 12)
STATION REPORT
==============
Site: Kaikoura
Pressure: 1000 NORMAL
Channels: 4

Status: ONLINE
Action: CHECK THE STATION

An ONLINE report runs to seven lines. Every other report runs to eight. You pass when each call prints exactly those lines and nothing else.

Rules
  • Bind the grade to a name, then test that name for the status. Do not run the pressure test a second time.
  • Do not type { or }. That rules out an f-string as well as a brace.
  • Join nothing with +. Hand the values to print and let the commas place the spaces.
  • Spell the operators out as words. The checker fails on && and ||.
  • Write elif in both chains, with no parentheses round a condition and no Tab characters.
  • Write no loop and no second function. Straight-line branching is the whole exercise.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.
